title: MIT's Gooey Solution: A Gel That Sticks Around to Deliver Drugs Right Where It Hurts
summary: Your esophagus is a muscular tunnel that shuttles food to your stomach in seconds. That's great for swallowing, but terrible for medicine—pills barely pause before plunging downward. For people with eosinophilic esophagitis, a food-allergy-driven inflammation that can seal the esophagus shut, or Crohn's disease, this is a daily struggle. Systemic drugs like infliximab, an antibody that blocks an inflammatory protein, can help, but they suppress the entire immune system, raising infection risks. Now, MIT engineers have designed a gel that could change that. The formulation, described in Nature Biomedical Engineering, is a polysaccharide hydrogel with a honey-like consistency. When swallowed, it clings to the esophageal lining. But the real magic is in two bile salts: sodium chenodeoxycholate and sodium cholate. These compounds temporarily pry apart tight junctions between epithelial cells—the normally impermeable barrier of the esophagus—by interacting with calcium ions. 'The hydrogel helps the formulation remain on the esophageal surface for longer, while the bile salts help increase transport across the tissue,' explains lead author Christina Karavasili. To find this duo, the team built a screening device mimicking the esophagus, with tissue pressed between two plates. They poured over 100 excipients through it, measuring permeability. The winning combo let infliximab pass through effectively in animal tests, and cell junctions resealed within three days. Senior author Giovanni Traverso, a gastroenterologist and MIT engineer, sees broader potential: 'This is a platform to enable the development of drug-delivery systems for the esophagus, which hasn't been possible before because the tools haven't existed.' The team is now optimizing the gel's adhesion time—long enough to work, short enough to avoid discomfort—and exploring other drugs. For patients who dread injections or systemic side effects, this gooey innovation could be a game-changer.
why_it_matters: This gel could transform how doctors treat localized diseases of the esophagus, making therapies safer by avoiding the whole-body immune suppression of current drugs. For young people interested in biomedical engineering, it shows how combining materials science with a deep understanding of biology can solve real-world problems—and perhaps one day they will be the ones designing the next drug-delivery platform.

background_read: The esophagus’s muscular contractions shove food into the stomach in seconds, making local drug delivery notoriously difficult. For decades, patients with eosinophilic esophagitis have relied on swallowed steroids or systemic immunosuppressants, which can cause widespread side effects because they affect the entire immune system.

Crohn’s disease, another inflammatory condition mentioned in the article, can affect any part of the digestive tract but often causes pain and narrowing similar to esophageal strictures. Infliximab, the drug used in the gel test, is a TNF-alpha inhibitor commonly prescribed for Crohn’s but taken by injection, posing risks like serious infections.

Nature Biomedical Engineering (where the study was published) is a high-impact journal that showcases cutting-edge engineering solutions for medical problems. The senior author Giovanni Traverso has previously developed other ingestible devices, including a capsule that can deliver insulin orally.

The use of bile salts to enhance drug absorption across mucosal barriers has been explored in the past for oral insulin delivery, but applying them to the esophagus is novel. Tight junctions resealing within three days is promising, though long-term safety needs careful study to ensure the barrier isn’t compromised permanently.
Article_Structure: PROBLEM: The esophagus moves food so fast that medicines barely stay in contact, leaving local diseases poorly treated.
└─ EXAMPLES: Eosinophilic esophagitis can seal the esophagus shut; Crohn’s disease patients face system-wide immune suppression from current drugs.
SOLUTION: MIT engineers designed a sticky hydrogel that clings to the esophageal lining.
├─ WHAT: A polysaccharide hydrogel with honey-like consistency.
└─ HOW: Two bile salts, sodium chenodeoxycholate and sodium cholate, temporarily pry open tight junctions between epithelial cells by interacting with calcium ions.
MECHANISM: The gel keeps the drug in place while the bile salts make the normally impermeable esophagus lining leaky enough for the drug to pass through.
TESTING: A custom screening device mimicked the esophagus, with tissue pressed between two plates, screening over 100 excipients.
├─ WHO: Lead author Christina Karavasili, senior author Giovanni Traverso.
└─ RESULT: Infliximab passed through effectively in animals, and cell junctions resealed within three days.
BROADER GOAL: Traverso calls it a platform for esophageal drug delivery that didn’t exist before.
NEXT STEPS: Optimize adhesion time—long enough to work but not cause discomfort—and explore other drugs.
IMPACT: For patients who dread injections or systemic side effects, this gooey innovation could be a game-changer.

perspectives.description: By delivering medicine directly where it’s needed, the gel could drastically reduce side effects from systemic drugs like infliximab, making treatment more tolerable for people with eosinophilic esophagitis or Crohn’s. The temporary opening of tight junctions offers a way to bypass one of the body’s toughest barriers without permanent damage.

Only animal tests have been done so far; repeatedly prying open tight junctions could compromise the esophagus’s protective barrier long-term, potentially allowing harmful substances or pathogens to enter the body. The hydrogel’s long-term wear on the delicate tissue and possible allergic reactions to bile salts need thorough investigation.

The difficulty of adhering drugs to rapidly moving mucosal surfaces has stumped scientists for decades. This approach builds on a broader trend of using bioadhesive materials and absorption enhancers, but similar attempts often fail in clinical trials because of unpredictable human physiology or manufacturing challenges.

If successful in humans, this platform might be adapted for other mucosal linings—like the intestines, bladder, or eyes—enabling a new class of non-invasive, targeted therapies. The focus on optimizing adhesion time hints at future gels that could deliver drugs over predetermined periods, opening doors to personalized dosing.
